questions.stem: A hospitalized client with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive. The capillary glucose is 38 mg/dL, and the client has an IV line. What should the nurse do first?

rationale.correct: Severe hypoglycemia: IV dextrose if there is IV access, or glucagon (IM, subcutaneous or intranasal) if not.

perOption.a: An unresponsive client can't swallow safely.
perOption.b: IV dextrose rapidly corrects severe hypoglycemia in a client with IV access.
perOption.c: Waiting delays treatment of a dangerous low.
perOption.d: Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.educationalObjective: Treat severe hypoglycemia in a client who can't swallow.

questions.stem: A client is shaky and sweaty with a glucose of 62 mg/dL. The client is alert and can swallow. Which snack should the nurse give?

rationale.correct: 15-15 rule: give 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still below 70 mg/dL.

perOption.a: This provides about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate.
perOption.b: Protein and fat raise glucose slowly.
perOption.c: The fat slows absorption.
perOption.d: Fast carbohydrate comes first; a snack or meal follows once the glucose recovers.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client with diabetes takes metoprolol. Why is this client at risk for not recognizing hypoglycemia?

options.text: Beta-blockers block warning signs such as a fast heartbeat and tremor
Beta-blockers make the client sleep more

rationale.correct: Beta-blockers can mask the adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia; clients should check their glucose more often.

perOption.a: Beta-blockers blunt the adrenergic response that causes palpitations and shakiness; sweating may still occur.
perOption.b: They can mask and prolong hypoglycemia rather than raise glucose.
perOption.c: Sweating isn't increased.
perOption.d: This isn't the mechanism.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize medications that mask hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Which prescription should the nurse start first?

rationale.correct: DKA treatment order: fluids, check potassium, IV insulin, then add dextrose once glucose falls to about 200 to 250 mg/dL.

perOption.a: Severe dehydration is the immediate threat; fluids restore perfusion and lower the glucose.
perOption.b: DKA needs IV regular insulin, started after fluids and a potassium check.
perOption.c: Bicarbonate is rarely used, only for severe acidosis.
perOption.d: The client isn't ready to eat.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with DKA on an insulin infusion now has a glucose of 220 mg/dL and an anion gap that hasn't closed. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin
Switch to subcutaneous insulin right away

rationale.correct: When glucose reaches about 200 to 250 mg/dL in DKA, add dextrose and continue insulin until the acidosis resolves.

perOption.a: Insulin is still needed to clear the ketones.
perOption.b: Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia while the insulin keeps clearing the ketoacidosis.
perOption.c: The switch happens when the gap closes and the client can eat.
perOption.d: Glucose is given IV to balance the infusion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Before starting an insulin infusion for DKA, the nurse sees the potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. Why is this important?

options.text: Insulin will raise the potassium to a dangerous level
Insulin moves potassium into cells, so the low potassium must be corrected first
The potassium doesn't matter in DKA
Low potassium means the DKA is resolving

rationale.correct: In DKA, total body potassium is low even if the blood level looks normal. Hold insulin if the potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L and replace it first.

perOption.a: Insulin lowers potassium.
perOption.b: Starting insulin with a potassium below 3.3 mEq/L can cause life-threatening hypokalemia.
perOption.c: Potassium shifts are a major risk.
perOption.d: This isn't a marker of resolution.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

exhibits.title: Nurse's note
exhibits.body: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 1 day. Deep, rapid breathing; fruity breath odor. Dry mucous membranes. Heart rate 124/min.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more typical of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS).

rows.text: Positive serum ketones with a pH of 7.15
Glucose of 940 mg/dL with serum osmolality of 350 mOsm/kg
Older adult with type 2 diabetes and gradual onset over days

rationale.correct: DKA = ketoacidosis, often type 1, rapid onset; HHS = extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration without significant ketosis, often type 2.

perOption.r1:c1: Ketoacidosis is the hallmark of DKA.
perOption.r1:c2: HHS has minimal ketones and a near-normal pH.
perOption.r2:c1: DKA glucose is usually lower, often 250 to 600 mg/dL.
perOption.r2:c2: Extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality define HHS.
perOption.r3:c1: Deep, rapid breathing compensates for metabolic acidosis.
perOption.r3:c2: HHS has little acidosis to compensate for.
perOption.r4:c1: DKA usually develops over hours, often in type 1 diabetes.
perOption.r4:c2: HHS develops slowly in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
perOption.r5:c1: Dehydration occurs in DKA, but it is usually more profound in HHS.
perOption.r5:c2: HHS causes extreme dehydration and neurologic changes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: An older adult with type 2 diabetes is admitted with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. What is the priority intervention?

rationale.correct: Fluid replacement is the cornerstone of HHS treatment, followed by insulin and electrolyte replacement.

perOption.a: Severe dehydration is the main problem in HHS.
perOption.b: HHS doesn't involve significant acidosis.
perOption.c: These are too slow and aren't appropriate in the acute phase.
perOption.d: This would worsen the dehydration.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has the flu and isn't eating much. Which statement shows a need for more teaching about sick-day management?

options.text: "I'll check my blood sugar every 3 to 4 hours."
"I'll skip my insulin because I'm not eating."
"I'll check for ketones if my sugar is over 240."

rationale.correct: Sick-day rules: keep taking insulin, monitor glucose and ketones, drink fluids and call the provider if vomiting continues or ketones are moderate to high.

perOption.a: Frequent checks are recommended.
perOption.b: Illness raises glucose; basal insulin must continue to prevent DKA.
perOption.c: Ketone testing is recommended.
perOption.d: Fluids prevent dehydration.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching foot care to a client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check your feet every day, using a mirror if needed
Wash and dry your feet well, especially between the toes
Always wear shoes or slippers, even indoors
Soak your feet in hot water every day
Use a heating pad on cold feet
Have toenails trimmed straight across or by a podiatrist

rationale.correct: Neuropathy hides injuries; daily inspection and protection prevent ulcers and amputations.

perOption.a: Daily checks catch injuries early.
perOption.b: Moisture between the toes promotes infection.
perOption.c: This protects numb feet from injury.
perOption.d: Soaking dries the skin, and reduced sensation risks burns.
perOption.f: This prevents ingrown nails and cuts.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client taking metformin calls the clinic. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: Mild diarrhea in the first week
Muscle pain, fast breathing and unusual sleepiness
Asking whether to take it with meals

rationale.correct: Metformin rarely causes lactic acidosis; the risk is higher with kidney impairment, contrast dye and heavy alcohol use.

perOption.a: GI upset is common early and usually improves.
perOption.b: These may be signs of lactic acidosis, a rare but serious adverse effect.
perOption.c: This is a minor side effect.
perOption.d: This is a teaching question; taking it with meals reduces GI upset.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is starting glipizide. Which adverse effect is most important for the nurse to teach about?

rationale.correct: Sulfonylureas: take before breakfast, don't skip meals and recognize and treat hypoglycemia.

perOption.a: Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia, especially if meals are skipped.
perOption.b: Sulfonylureas often cause weight gain.
perOption.c: This is associated with metformin.
perOption.d: These are associated with SGLT2 inhibitors.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

options.text: "Report genital itching or discharge and stay well hydrated."
"This medication commonly causes hypoglycemia when taken alone."
"Take it only when your sugar is high."

rationale.correct: SGLT2 inhibitors: genital infections, UTIs, dehydration and rare euglycemic DKA.

perOption.a: SGLT2 inhibitors put glucose into the urine, raising the risk of genital yeast infections and dehydration.
perOption.b: Alone, SGLT2 inhibitors rarely cause hypoglycemia.
perOption.c: It is taken daily.
perOption.d: Hydration is important.

questions.stem: Which history would contraindicate starting semaglutide?

options.text: Family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma

rationale.correct: GLP-1 agonists: watch for pancreatitis and GI effects; they are contraindicated with a history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.

perOption.a: GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a warning about thyroid C-cell tumors and are contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.
perOption.b: Obesity is an indication.
perOption.c: Type 2 diabetes is an indication.
perOption.d: This isn't a contraindication.

questions.stem: A client's hemoglobin A1C is 9.2%. What does this result tell the nurse?

options.text: Glucose control has been poor over the past 2 to 3 months
The client's diabetes is well controlled

rationale.correct: A1C shows long-term glucose control; a target below 7% is common for adults.

perOption.a: The A1C reflects average glucose over about 3 months; most adults aim for below 7%.
perOption.b: A1C doesn't reflect a single day.
perOption.c: 9.2% is well above target.
perOption.d: 6.5% or higher is diagnostic of diabetes.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client who takes NPH insulin at bedtime has high fasting glucose each morning. A 0300 check shows 52 mg/dL. Which explanation is most likely?

rationale.correct: Somogyi effect: low at 0300, high in the morning, so reduce the evening insulin or add a snack. Dawn phenomenon: normal at 0300, high in the morning, so adjust the timing or dose.

perOption.a: In the dawn phenomenon, the 0300 glucose is normal or high.
perOption.b: Nighttime hypoglycemia triggers counter-regulatory hormones that cause rebound morning hyperglycemia.
perOption.c: This doesn't explain the nighttime low.
perOption.d: More insulin would worsen the nighttime low.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes checks the glucose before exercising, and it is 290 mg/dL with moderate urine ketones. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "Go ahead and exercise to lower your sugar."
"Don't exercise now; follow your plan for high glucose and ketones."
"Exercise is never safe for people with type 1 diabetes."

rationale.correct: Avoid vigorous exercise when the glucose is above about 250 mg/dL with ketones. Carry fast carbohydrate during exercise.

perOption.a: Exercise with ketosis can worsen hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis.
perOption.b: Exercise is postponed when ketones are present.
perOption.c: The glucose is already high.
perOption.d: Exercise is beneficial when glucose is safe.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe exercise for diabetes.

questions.stem: Which result confirms a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

options.text: Fasting plasma glucose of 132 mg/dL on two separate days
Random glucose of 160 mg/dL without symptoms

rationale.correct: Diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose 126 or higher, A1C 6.5% or higher, 2-hour OGTT 200 or higher, or random glucose 200 or higher with symptoms.

perOption.a: A fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed by repeat testing, is diagnostic.
perOption.b: A random glucose needs to be 200 or higher with symptoms.
perOption.c: This is in the prediabetes range (5.7% to 6.4%).
perOption.d: This is prediabetes (100 to 125).

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

perOption.a: This is too long between exams.
perOption.b: Annual screening finds retinopathy early, when treatment can prevent vision loss.
perOption.c: Early retinopathy has no symptoms.
perOption.d: Screening continues for life.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is NPO for surgery in the morning. What should the nurse do about the client's usual insulin?

options.text: Hold all insulin until the client eats again
Contact the provider for an adjusted basal insulin dose and monitor glucose closely
Give the full mealtime insulin as usual
Switch the client to an oral diabetes drug

rationale.correct: Type 1 diabetes always needs basal insulin; adjust it while NPO and monitor glucose closely.

perOption.a: People with type 1 diabetes always need basal insulin to prevent DKA.
perOption.b: The basal dose is usually reduced, not stopped, while the client is NPO, with frequent glucose checks.
perOption.c: Mealtime insulin without food causes hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: Oral drugs don't work in type 1 diabetes.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client with diabetes who takes insulin asks about drinking alcohol. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll drink only on an empty stomach so it doesn't raise my sugar."
"If I drink, I'll have it with food and check my sugar, including before bed."
"I'll take extra insulin when I drink."
"Alcohol has no effect on my blood sugar."

rationale.correct: Alcohol can cause delayed hypoglycemia; drink in moderation with food and monitor glucose.

perOption.a: Alcohol without food increases the risk of hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: Alcohol blocks the liver from releasing glucose; delayed hypoglycemia can happen overnight.
perOption.c: This increases the hypoglycemia risk.
perOption.d: Alcohol can cause hypoglycemia.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client's insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio is 1 unit per 15 g. The correction factor is 1 unit for every 50 mg/dL above 150 mg/dL. Before a meal containing 75 g of carbohydrate, the glucose is 250 mg/dL. How many units of rapid-acting insulin should the client take?

rationale.correct: Meal dose: 75 g ÷ 15 g = 5 units. Correction: (250 − 150) ÷ 50 = 2 units. Total: 5 + 2 = 7 units.
references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
